app.title: Breathe
app.subtitle: Find a comfortable rhythm, one breath at a time.

detail.evidenceGuide: Evidence labels summarize the cited research, not a formal clinical grade or a validation of this app.
detail.protocolNote: This timer is a practice guide. Its exact timing and session length have not been clinically tested.
detail.generalSafety: Breathe gently. Stop and return to your normal breathing if you feel dizzy, uncomfortable, or more anxious. Breathing practice does not replace medical care.

congrats.title: A moment for yourself
congrats.message:
Notice how you feel.
You can finish whenever you need.

box.name: Box Breathing
box.tagline: A steady rhythm for a moment of calm
box.science: A 2023 trial included box breathing in a month of daily five-minute practice. A 2026 pilot in 47 students found less acute anxiety after one minute of box breathing or sighing than after a passive control.
box.mechanism: Equal phases structure your attention and slow the breathing cycle. The pauses are optional for comfort; they are not a test of lung capacity.
steps: Sit comfortably and relax your shoulders.
Inhale gently through your nose for 4 seconds.
Pause for up to 4 seconds, only while comfortable.
Exhale gently for 4 seconds.
Pause for up to 4 seconds. Use Breathe now whenever you need to end a hold.
Begin with a few comfortable cycles. Never force a breath or hold.
benefits: May ease anxious feelings with regular practice.
Offers a simple counting rhythm to anchor your attention.
box.limitations: Evidence remains limited. A 2025 comparison found no meaningful immediate mood change. Attention results in the 2026 pilot were mixed, including slower responses. Better performance under pressure and lasting benefits are not established.
box.safety: If the holds feel uncomfortable, stop and choose diaphragmatic breathing without holds.

fourSevenEight.name: 4-7-8 Technique
fourSevenEight.tagline: A slow pattern with an extended exhale
fourSevenEight.science: A 2022 study of 43 healthy young adults observed immediate changes in heart rate and blood pressure after 4-7-8 breathing. A 2025 comparison found larger HRV increases with six breaths per minute.
fourSevenEight.mechanism: The pattern combines a slow inhale, a pause, and a longer exhale. Changes in breathing can affect heart-rate rhythms; a specific CO2 or vagus-nerve explanation is not proven for this app.
steps: Sit comfortably.
Inhale gently through your nose for 4 seconds.
Hold for up to 7 seconds only if comfortable.
Exhale gently through your mouth for 8 seconds; do not force the air out.
Start with 4 cycles. Stop sooner if you need to; more cycles are not necessarily better.
benefits: May temporarily lower heart rate after practice in some healthy adults.
Offers a structured routine for winding down.
fourSevenEight.limitations: These short studies do not show that 4-7-8 treats insomnia, resets the nervous system, or has unique long-term benefits.
fourSevenEight.safety: The 7-second hold can feel demanding. If it feels uncomfortable, stop and choose a technique without holds.

diaphragmatic.name: Diaphragmatic Breathing
diaphragmatic.science: A small randomized study found improvements in attention, negative mood, and cortisol after eight weeks of training. A 2019 review found encouraging stress results in three studies, with important limitations.
diaphragmatic.mechanism: Let the diaphragm move naturally as you breathe, with gentle movement around the lower ribs and belly. Avoid taking unusually large breaths or trying to keep the chest completely still.
steps: Sit comfortably or lie on your back.
Rest a hand on your belly or lower ribs.
Inhale gently for 5 seconds, allowing the belly and lower ribs to move.
Exhale gently for 5 seconds without squeezing all the air out.
Use a smaller, comfortable breath rather than the deepest breath possible.
Choose a comfortable session length; the guided duration is shown below.
benefits: May reduce perceived stress with regular practice.
May support sustained attention; findings are preliminary.
diaphragmatic.limitations: Training programs differed, and the evidence is small. An immediate cortisol reduction from this short session is not established.
diaphragmatic.safety: Comfort matters more than depth. Return to normal breathing if following the pace feels difficult.

resonance.name: Slow / Resonance Breathing
resonance.tagline: A gentle pace to explore HRV and relaxation
resonance.science: A 2024 meta-analysis found short-term increases in HRV with slow breathing. Research on HRV biofeedback also supports stress reduction, but biofeedback uses physiological measurements that this timer does not provide.
resonance.mechanism: Breathing influences the natural speeding and slowing of the heart. Many adults have a resonance rate around 4.5-6.5 breaths per minute. This 5.5-second inhale and exhale pattern is about 5.45 breaths per minute, without inter-cycle gaps.
steps: Sit or lie comfortably.
Inhale gently for 5.5 seconds.
Exhale gently for 5.5 seconds.
Continue smoothly without holding at either end.
Use comfortable-sized breaths; slow breathing can still cause over-breathing if breaths are too large.
Choose a comfortable session length; the guided duration is shown below.
benefits: Can increase HRV while breathing slowly.
May support relaxation and stress management with regular practice.
resonance.limitations: A higher HRV during paced breathing does not prove better recovery the next day. Your personal resonance frequency cannot be determined from a fixed timer.
resonance.safety: Keep breaths gentle and unforced. If this pace feels too slow, stop and return to a comfortable natural rhythm.

wimHof.name: Wim Hof-style Breathing
wimHof.tagline: Advanced pattern; health benefits remain uncertain
wimHof.science: A 2024 review of eight trials found signals in inflammatory markers, but small samples, study bias, and varied protocols limit confidence. Some studies combined breathing with cold exposure and other training.
wimHof.mechanism: Rapid, deep breathing lowers carbon dioxide and changes blood chemistry. A later breath hold can reduce oxygen levels. These physiological changes are not, by themselves, evidence of a health benefit.
steps: Review the safety information before considering this advanced pattern.
The animation guides 30 breaths over 45 seconds. Do not force your breathing.
After the exhale, pause only while comfortable. Use Breathe now at the first urge to breathe.
Do not wait for the 60-second timer to finish if you need to breathe sooner.
Take an easy recovery inhale over about 3 seconds, followed by an optional pause of up to 15 seconds. Use Breathe now to end it sooner.
Stop immediately if you feel dizzy or unwell.
benefits: Researchers are investigating changes in inflammatory responses; benefits for everyday health are not established.
wimHof.limitations: This does not show that the app boosts immunity, prevents illness, or improves sports recovery. This breathing timer is not the full Wim Hof Method.
wimHof.safety: Hyperventilation and holds can cause fainting. Never practice in water, while driving, standing, or anywhere fainting could cause harm. The 60-second timer is not a target: use Breathe now at the first urge to breathe. Do not practice during pregnancy. Seek clinical advice first if you have a health condition.

buteyko.name: Buteyko-style Breathing
buteyko.tagline: Breathing retraining; evidence comes from asthma care
buteyko.science: A Cochrane review included 22 asthma studies using several breathing methods, including Buteyko. It found some quality-of-life benefits, with variable evidence quality.
buteyko.mechanism: Buteyko programs teach changes in breathing habits, often emphasizing gentle nasal breathing. This app demonstrates a simplified pattern, not an individualized clinical program.
steps: Sit comfortably and breathe naturally through your nose if comfortable.
Take a small, gentle inhale for 3 seconds.
Exhale gently for 3 seconds.
Pause only until the first urge to breathe. Use Breathe now to finish the pause sooner.
Return to easy, comfortable breathing. Do not force shallow breaths or air hunger.
The app does not measure a control-pause baseline or diagnose your breathing.
benefits: Breathing retraining may improve quality of life for some adults with asthma.
buteyko.evidenceLabel: Evidence is specific to clinical programs
buteyko.limitations: The findings do not validate this fixed control-pause timer or prove general CO2-tolerance benefits. A timed pause is not a lung-health or fitness test.
buteyko.safety: Use alongside your usual care; never change prescribed inhalers based on this app. Stop a pause at the first urge to breathe, using Breathe now; the 20-second timer is not a target. Do not create distressing air hunger.

cyclicSighing.name: Gentle Cyclic Sighing
cyclicSighing.tagline: Two easy inhales, one longer exhale
benefits: Promising research for mood and everyday stress management.
cyclicSighing.science: A 2023 trial found encouraging mood and breathing-rate results from five minutes of daily practice over one month. A 2026 pilot in 47 students found less acute anxiety after one-minute sighing or box breathing than after a passive control.
cyclicSighing.limitations: The app uses a gentle 3-1-6 adaptation that has not been tested as delivered here. Early trials do not establish lasting benefits, a best technique, or better attention; the 2026 pilot also found slower attention-test responses.
cyclicSighing.mechanism: The second inhale is a small top-up before an easy, longer exhale. Comfort matters more than filling your lungs.
cyclicSighing.safety: Keep both inhales comfortable. Stop if you feel dizzy or uncomfortable; ordinary belly breathing is another option.
steps: Sit comfortably and relax your shoulders.
Inhale gently through your nose for 3 seconds.
Add a small second inhale for about 1 second, only if comfortable.
Exhale slowly and easily for 6 seconds.
Repeat without holds or straining. You can stop at any time.

extendedExhale.name: Longer Exhale
extendedExhale.tagline: A gentle rhythm for winding down
benefits: Offers a comfortable, hold-free wind-down routine.
extendedExhale.evidenceLabel: Supported as slow breathing; ratio is not superior
extendedExhale.science: Slow-breathing studies include 4-second inhales and 6-second exhales. A longer exhale has not consistently increased HRV more than equal inhale and exhale.
extendedExhale.limitations: This is not an insomnia treatment. The best-feeling ratio can differ from person to person.
extendedExhale.mechanism: A slightly longer exhale gives you time to release the breath without holding or pushing.
extendedExhale.safety: Never force a long exhale. Return to your normal rhythm if this pace feels difficult.
steps: Sit or lie comfortably.
Inhale gently for 4 seconds.
Exhale softly for 6 seconds.
Flow directly into the next comfortable inhale, with no holds.

humming.name: Gentle Humming
humming.tagline: A soft sound to follow on the exhale
benefits: May offer a pleasant sensory focus during a breathing pause.
humming.science: A 2025 pilot found similar HRV and self-rated feelings during humming and slow breathing. It did not establish that humming works better.
humming.limitations: This small study does not establish long-term health benefits. The app’s 4-6 pace is a practice adaptation.
humming.mechanism: A soft hum adds a sound and vibration you can notice as you exhale.
humming.safety: Hum quietly without squeezing the throat or running out of air. Skip the sound if it feels uncomfortable.
steps: Relax your jaw, neck, and shoulders.
Inhale gently through your nose for 4 seconds.
Exhale for up to 6 seconds with a soft “mmm”, lips comfortably together.
Take the next comfortable breath without holding. The sound is optional.

checkin.title: How do you feel today?
checkin.intro: Choose what fits right now. We’ll suggest a gentle place to start.
checkin.holds: I’m comfortable with gentle breath holds
checkin.privacy: Your check-in stays in this tab unless you choose to save a session reflection. No account needed.
checkin.boundary: Suggestions follow your preferences, not a medical assessment. Choose what feels comfortable.

reasons.tense: You feel tense. A gentle sighing pattern offers an exhale-focused pause; you can choose belly breathing instead.
reasons.busy: You want a mental pause without holds. An easy belly-breathing rhythm gives your attention a simple anchor.
reasons.busyWithHolds: You’re comfortable with holds and want a mental pause. Box breathing offers a clear counting rhythm; holds can end whenever you need.
reasons.sleep: You want to wind down. Try a comfortable, longer exhale without holding your breath. This is a relaxation routine, not an insomnia treatment.
reasons.low: You feel low on energy. Start with gentle breathing rather than an intense exercise. Rest may be more useful if you’re tired.
reasons.curious: You’re exploring. Try a smooth slow-breathing rhythm or humming if the sound feels pleasant.

guide.readyCue: Sit comfortably. Let your breathing settle.
guide.pauseCue: Breathe normally. Resume when you feel ready.
guide.hiddenPause: Paused while you were away. Breathe normally before resuming.
guide.holdNote: This is a maximum, not a target. Breathe whenever you need.

cue.inhale: Breathe in gently through your nose.
cue.topUp: Add one small, comfortable second inhale.
cue.exhale: Let the air out slowly and easily.
cue.holdFull: Rest briefly with air in. No straining.
cue.holdEmpty: Rest briefly after exhaling. No straining.
cue.retention: Pause only while comfortable. Breathe as soon as you need.
cue.power: Inhale and release at your own comfort. Stop if you feel dizzy.
cue.easy: Let your own easy breathing rhythm return.
cue.bellyIn: Let your belly expand gently. Keep your shoulders relaxed.
cue.bellyOut: Let your belly settle as the air leaves. No pushing.

box.name: The four-sided path
box.description: Follow one side for each phase: inhale, pause, exhale, pause. The marker counts time during pauses too.

fourSevenEight.name: The 4–7–8 timing ring
fourSevenEight.description: Each ring segment follows the phase duration shown below. The center opens on inhale, rests during the pause, and closes on exhale.

diaphragmatic.name: Belly & diaphragm schematic
diaphragmatic.description: The lower belly expands gently on inhale as the gold diaphragm curve lowers. Both return on exhale. This is a simplified movement cue.

resonance.name: The breathing tide
resonance.description: Rise with the tide on inhale and settle with it on exhale, without pauses. This shows your breathing pace, not an HRV measurement.

wimHof.name: Breath-count beads
wimHof.description: One bead for each of the 30 guided breaths. The center rests during retention. Holds end whenever you need to breathe.

buteyko.name: The resting feather
buteyko.description: Small movements accompany the gentle inhale and exhale. The feather rests during the optional pause and natural breathing; it is not a target to beat.

cyclicSighing.name: The two inhale chambers
cyclicSighing.description: One easy inhale opens the larger chamber; a small top-up opens the smaller one. Both release together during the longer exhale.

extendedExhale.name: The slow hourglass
extendedExhale.description: The upper bowl fills during the {{inhale}}-second inhale and releases during the {{exhale}}-second exhale. Keep the breath comfortable.

humming.name: The humming bowl
humming.description: The pearl opens for your inhale. Gentle vibration arcs appear only during the humming exhale; they show sound, not extra breaths.

box.inhale: The center opens. Follow the first side.
box.hold: The center stays still. The marker counts the pause.
box.exhale: The center settles. Follow the third side.

fourSevenEight.hold: The center stays still for the optional pause.

resonance.exhale: Settle with the tide, then begin the next easy breath.

wimHof.power: One bead for each guided breath.
wimHof.retention: The center rests. Breathe whenever you need.
wimHof.hold: The center stays still. End the hold whenever you need.

buteyko.inhale: A small movement for a gentle inhale.
buteyko.exhale: A small movement for an easy exhale.
buteyko.hold: The feather rests. Breathe whenever you need.
buteyko.easy: The feather rests. Follow your own natural rhythm.

cyclicSighing.inhale: 1 · One easy inhale opens the larger chamber.
cyclicSighing.topUp: 2 · One small top-up opens the smaller chamber.
cyclicSighing.exhale: 3 · Both chambers release in one slow exhale.

extendedExhale.exhale: {{exhale}} seconds out · upper bowl empties more slowly

humming.inhale: The pearl opens. Breathe in quietly.
humming.hum: The arcs show your soft “mmm” during this exhale.

audio.title: Sound & music
audio.intro: Choose a quiet background for your practice. Start low and adjust to comfort. Your choice is saved on this device.
audio.originalTones: Ambient tones and breathing chimes are created by the app, without a third-party music recording.
audio.recordingNote: Nature recordings are hosted with the app and blended for smooth loops. No streaming service or account is needed.

status.ready: Background sound starts with your practice. Set breathing cues to 0% to turn off the chimes.
status.playing: Playing softly. You can change the sound or volume at any time.
status.paused: Sound is paused with your practice.
status.muted: All sounds are muted. Use the speaker button to unmute.
status.unavailable: This sound could not play. Try another sound or continue in silence.

lesson.invitation: Explore how the diaphragm and belly move before you practice.
lesson.title: Where does the movement happen?
lesson.intro: Compare the two positions, then turn to the side to see the depth of the diaphragm’s dome and the belly’s movement.
lesson.inhaleExplanation: The diaphragm contracts, lowers and becomes flatter. Let the belly expand gently, with relaxed shoulders.
lesson.exhaleExplanation: The diaphragm relaxes and returns upward. Let the belly settle without pushing the air out.
lesson.loading: Loading the optional movement view. The 2D illustration is ready.
lesson.fallback: The 3D view is unavailable. Compare the same positions in this 2D illustration.
lesson.reduced: Reduced motion: compare still positions in 2D.
lesson.note: A simplified illustration with exaggerated movement. Your lungs sit above the diaphragm; green shows abdominal movement, not air entering the belly. Breathe normally while exploring; these positions are not breathing targets.

personal.title: My practice
personal.naturalCue: Let your breathing find its own comfortable rhythm. There is no inhale or exhale target.
personal.naturalVisual: The illustration stays still. The time shown is session time, not the length of a breath.
personal.paceDescription: Your phase lengths: {{pattern}} seconds. Choose a pace that feels easy.
personal.fixedAdvanced: Advanced patterns keep their reference timing. You can end any hold immediately, or choose unpaced breathing.
personal.adaptation: This is a personal adaptation. Research on the reference technique does not validate this particular pace or unpaced session.
personal.noHoldAlternative: Choose a gentle practice without holds
personal.reminderNote: On the website, download a calendar file after saving and import it into your calendar to receive reminders while the app is closed. The file includes your routine name and schedule. Android can schedule local notifications; delivery may be delayed by battery settings. Manage imported reminders in your calendar; removing a routine here does not remove its calendar event.
personal.chooseDays: Choose a valid time and at least one day.
personal.routineLimit: You can save up to 30 routines. Remove one to make room.
personal.afterIntro: Optional. There is no right outcome, and stopping early is okay.
personal.feedbackPrivacy: Saving is optional and off by default. Your choice and practice details stay in this browser or app. No account or upload. Leaving this unchecked skips saving this reflection.
personal.feedbackSaved: Saved on this device. Thank you for noticing how you feel.
personal.feedbackThanks: Thank you for checking in. This reflection was not saved.
personal.localIntro: Your routines and optional reflections stay on this device. Browser data can be cleared by your device; export a copy if you want to keep one.
personal.noRoutines: Save a favorite or a routine from a practice’s settings.
personal.reflectionCount: {{count}} saved reflections · showing up to 12 recent entries
personal.observations: These are personal observations, without a claim that a practice caused a health change. Switching off saved reflections here deletes them; routines remain.
personal.exportError: The export could not be saved. Try again.
personal.due: A moment for yourself: {{name}}. Open My practice when it suits you.
personal.helpfulBefore: You previously reported feeling more settled after {{name}}. It is offered first within these gentle choices.
personal.accessIntro: All settings are optional. Quiet mode turns off sound, spoken guidance, and vibration together.
personal.sensoryNote: Voice and vibration depend on the device. Spoken instructions do not work as screen-off guidance on the website. Pause, stop, or leave the app to end cues.
personal.voiceSample: Find a comfortable position. Let your breathing settle.
personal.nativeSensory: Android uses available on-device speech and vibration. These cues are optional.
personal.webSensory: Browser speech uses an available device voice; offline availability varies. Some browsers do not support vibration. The page stays usable without either.
personal.memoryOnly: Your browser cannot save changes right now. These tools work for this visit; export anything you want to keep.
personal.notificationPermission: Routine saved. Enable notification permission in Android to receive its reminder.
personal.reminderScheduled: Reminder settings saved on this device.
personal.reminderError: Routine saved, but Android could not schedule its reminder. You can edit it and try again.

offline.title: Install & offline
offline.intro: Core practices are saved for offline use after a successful online visit. Sound recordings are optional downloads.
offline.installHelp: Use your browser’s Install app or Add to Home screen menu if no install button appears. An update waits until you choose it outside practice.
offline.preparing: Preparing the offline app. Keep this page open while the first download finishes, then reload once.
offline.ready: Core practices are ready offline on this device.
offline.offline: You are offline. Your saved practices and downloaded sounds are available.
offline.unavailable: Offline setup is unavailable here. You can still use the app while connected.
offline.native: The Android app includes the practices, lesson, and sounds for offline use.
offline.soundNote: Synthesized ambient tones need no download. Offline recordings use device storage and can be removed here. Voice availability depends on installed device voices.
offline.downloadFailed: The sound could not be saved. Check your connection and try again.

context.title: Today’s context
context.intro: Optional context for your own reflection. Your feelings and preferences still guide the practice suggestions.
context.nativeIntro: Choose which records to share, then approve Android’s Health Connect permissions. Read-only, on demand, up to the last 7 days. No background access or upload; records stay in this screen’s memory.
context.webIntro: Automatic Health Connect access needs the Android companion. This website cannot read your Fitbit records. You can add a little context manually below.
context.chooseTypes: Choose at least one record type.
context.error: Could not read Health Connect. Check the provider, permissions, and data availability, then try again.
context.boundary: Availability depends on what Fitbit or another source actually shares. Missing values are not zero. Timestamps and sources matter; these records do not identify a medical condition or establish which breathing technique will help. Sleep is the duration of the latest recorded session, not a sleep-quality score.

status.unavailable: Health Connect is unavailable on this device.
status.updateRequired: Install or update Health Connect before connecting.
status.denied: No selected records were shared. You can use every breathing practice without connecting.
